text: A finished build with nothing written down forces you to reconstruct your own reasoning on the spot, in an interview, for something you built weeks ago. A short written document fixes that — not a report for someone else to read cover to cover, but a reference you've already written once, so when you're asked to walk through it, you're recalling a story you've already told clearly.

Four components make that document hold up. First, the business problem — a real situation, stated before any mention of the solution: not 'built a Flow Designer automation,' but 'manual ticket routing meant every request sat in one queue until someone manually triaged it.' Second, and most often skipped: the design decisions, and why. Course 13 introduced the Architecture Decision Record habit for exactly this reason — a decision without its reasoning is just a fact, easily second-guessed. What real alternatives did you consider, and what actually drove the choice you made?

Third, what was actually built — kept brief and factual, since an interviewer looking at a screen share can often see this part for themselves. Fourth, and the component that most separates a thoughtful candidate from one just reciting a project: what you'd do differently with more time or scale. A Personal Developer Instance never forces you to handle real user volume or real governance friction. Naming those limits honestly, and saying what you'd change at real scale, is exactly the judgment an architect-level interview is testing for.

This same four-part structure applies going forward, not just backward. You're about to build a new capstone starting in Chapter 4 — scoped to a large organization, worked through across requirements, build, and presentation. Write your ADRs as you go, the same habit course 13 taught, so the reasoning is captured while you still remember it, not reconstructed after the fact.

Business problem, design decisions and why, what was built, what you'd change at scale — write it as you go. Next up, Chapter 4: Capstone Overview, the 5,000-employee organization. Now you'll build the flagship project you just learned how to showcase.
